- ‌**pachamama** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Pachamama.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Pachamama ‌place ​earth, harvest, ​mother ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Pachamama ‌appears ​in incan ‌tradition ​as ​earth, harvest, ​mother. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Mother ​Earth", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Pachamama ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Pachamama ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Pachamama ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Pachamama, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​earth ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Pachamama** ​(*pachamama*) — ‌Earth, Harvest, ‌Mother · ​The ​fertile earth ​beneath every ​step ​— belongs ‌to the ​Incan tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Earth, ‌Harvest, Mother". ​The name ​means ​"Mother Earth"[^1].

​**Pachamama** is ​the ‌living earth ​of the ‌Andes — ​mother ‌of harvests, ​herds, and ‌households, ​the ground ‌that feeds ​and the ​ground ‌that opens. ‌Hers is ‌a ​religion of ​**reciprocity**: nothing ‌is taken ​from ​the earth ‌without payment ​returned ​to it. ‌She is ​not a ‌goddess ​of temples ​alone but ​of ​every furrow, ‌kitchen, and ‌burial in ​the ‌Inca world ​and beyond.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Pachamama** ‌and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/pachamama/). The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— ​a description ​computed from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*pachamama* contains ‌the same ​letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Pachamama** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken form. ‌Etymologically ​the name ‌means ​"Mother Earth"[^1].

‌The ​canonical spelling ​**Pachamama** ​matches the ​conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *pachamama* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. ‌The editorial ‌work ​is to ​fix ‌one reviewed ​reference ​spelling, preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ‌keep the ​original ‌evidence visible. ​The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ‌description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself.

meditation.body:
Pachamama ​teaches a ‌grammar the ‌modern ​world has ​largely forgotten: ​the dative ​case ​of the ‌earth. English ​says ​we *use* ‌land; Quechua ​says ‌we are ​*given by* ‌it. ​The difference ​is not ​semantic decoration. ​A ​civilization that ‌thinks of ​soil ‌as property ​eventually exhausts ‌it; ​one that ‌thinks of ​soil ‌as a ​mother who ​must be ‌fed ‌plans in ‌centuries. The ​Andean ​payment — ‌a splash ​of ​chicha, a ‌pinch of ​coca ​— looks ‌small until ​you notice ‌it ​has never ​stopped, through ​conquest, ​evangelization, republics, ‌and revolutions.

‌To ​speak her ‌name is ​to ​be reminded ‌that reciprocity ‌is not ‌charity ‌but physics: ​every withdrawal ‌is ​a debt, ​and the ​earth ‌always collects. ​Her modern ​constitutional ​career, granting ‌standing to ​mountains and ​rivers, ​is only ‌the old ​kitchen ‌theology written ​large. Pachamama ‌asks ​each of ‌us the ‌question ​the chronicles ​recorded: what ​have you ​paid ‌the ground ‌that carries ​you?[^1]
